author: agent
text:
Re-read after 0.54.2. The correction recorded below still holds - the docstring no longer claims body-hash stamping, which was false after stamping unified on stamp_for.

What changed: this passes repo_root to stamp_for now, so the MCP write path stamps against the WORKING TREE like the CLI and console paths do. All three still route through the single stamp_for; the argument is the only difference, and that is the point - the drift this function's own history records (CLI stamping body_hash while agent_meta stamped logic_hash) came from two implementations, not two arguments.

Consequence worth knowing at this coordinate: an agent that edits code and then writes a note NO LONGER has to re-index first for the note to be fresh. Before 0.54.2 the note carried the pre-edit hash and was stale the moment the index caught up, which made the supersede-what-you-staled rule unable to do its job even when followed exactly.

If the ref has vanished from the working tree, stamp_for raises GhostEntity and this surface should let it become a clear error rather than writing a note that can never be fresh.

author: agent
text:
Re-read at 0.63.0. The stamping claims below all still hold and were checked: this passes repo_root to stamp_for so the MCP write path stamps against the WORKING TREE exactly like the CLI and console paths, all three still route through the single stamp_for, and an agent that edits then writes a note still does not have to re-index first.

WHAT CHANGED: this accepts `replaces`, and until now it could not.

THE GAP IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE OF WHO IT AFFECTED. cmd_meta has taken --replaces since it was added; the MCP door never did. `replaces` is the field that records WHY a belief changed - the thing review renders as "because: ..." and the one part of a supersession nobody can reconstruct from the texts alone. Agents wrote 68 percent of this map's knowledge entries, so the surface that produces most of the knowledge was the one that could not say why any of it changed. The author of this session hit it directly and shelled out to the CLI to write supersede reasons that should have gone through here.

HOW IT SURVIVED: the surface-parity test walked mcp.TOOLS and demanded a CLI and --json door for each, and nothing walked the other way. A capability that existed for a human and not for an agent was structurally invisible to the guard. That test is bidirectional as of this release, and the reverse direction immediately named `review` - an agent could not see what its own change did to the knowledge it was being asked to maintain. Note that the reverse test checks DOORS, not PARAMETERS: it would not have found this one. A tool can be present on every surface and still be unable to express the thing that matters.
